title: June deliberations distinguish a volatile GDP contraction from a case for cutting rates
summary: Published on 24 June, this account explains why the Governing Council kept the overnight rate at 2.25% on 10 June despite two quarters of negative GDP readings and consumer inflation close to 3%. The Council saw a weak economy operating below capacity, but no clear evidence of a deep, broad or sustained recession. Core inflation remained close to 2%. Raising rates to counter petrol alone could hit spending after the shock had subsided, while lowering rates into a prolonged energy disruption could make higher costs easier to pass on. The hold reflected those opposing timing risks rather than a judgement that output and inflation had both met their objectives (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Policy decision).

First-quarter GDP edged down 0.1% compared with a 1.5% increase projected in April. Government spending dropped 2.5%, with the timing of spending on weapons systems important. Household spending grew 1.4% and per-capita consumption grew 2%. Housing weakened and exports fell, while strong imports accompanied inventory rebuilding. Over the year to the first quarter, aggregate activity had been roughly flat and more than half of industries posted some growth in the latest quarter. Reading two negative GDP prints in isolation would therefore overlook private consumption, the concentration of the forecast error and the breadth of activity. These details did not remove slack, but they changed the case for an immediate rate cut (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The preliminary April GDP estimate pointed to an increase of 0.4% month-on-month. Energy exports rose with stronger prices, alongside gains in motor vehicles and machinery. Early indicators suggested some stabilisation in housing and improving intentions for investment and hiring. May’s employment jump pulled unemployment to 6.6%, though employment was little changed since the start of the year and unemployment had remained in a 6½–7% range. Council treated both the negative GDP print and the strong one-month jobs number with caution. A rebound in the next quarter, especially following unusually low government spending, would answer a different question from whether labour demand had become strong enough to eliminate spare capacity (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

April CPI inflation of 2.8% was close to the earlier projection of around 3%. Higher petrol prices and refining margins contributed, as did the removal from the year-over-year comparison of the previous April’s consumer carbon-tax change. The trimmed and median CPI measures were both near 2%, the proportion of components increasing above 3% fell towards its historical average, and rent and food inflation slowed. First-quarter business survey evidence showed higher near-term expected inflation and anchored longer-term beliefs. There was no newer Bank survey at the decision date. A researcher should therefore pair the new CPI observation with the actual vintage of the expectations survey rather than treating the two as simultaneous measures of how households and firms responded (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The conflict, now in its fourth month, affected energy, shipping, fertiliser and other petrochemicals. Council considered a decisive end with markedly lower oil, escalation and a renewed price jump, or a ceasefire that partially restored transport while preserving uncertainty and somewhat higher prices. New supply routes and stock drawdowns could mitigate shortages but would take time or eventually run out. AI investment supported US growth and production in parts of Asia even while energy-importing economies weakened. Global demand for Canadian goods thus depended on trading partner and industry. Domestic financial conditions had eased with stronger equities and little change in Canadian yields, while the Canadian dollar depreciated against the US dollar as relative growth and expectations for the policy-rate differential shifted (International economy).

The policy decision turned on the lag from the overnight rate to spending and prices. If oil fell promptly, a pre-emptive hike might reach the economy just as its motivating price pressure disappeared. If prolonged high energy costs became incorporated into prices across sectors, waiting for conclusive signs of persistence could ultimately force a more aggressive tightening. The observable distinction was whether the shock continued to be concentrated in petrol or began to change pricing behaviour more broadly. Excess supply and a slack labour market could limit pass-through even as direct headline inflation remained elevated. Conversely, disruption to supply chains could continue after oil prices eased, so spot crude alone was insufficient to resolve the issue (Considerations for monetary policy).

Trade negotiations created a second, potentially simultaneous, risk. A favourable North American agreement could encourage investment, while delays or a worsening of restrictions could spread distress beyond directly affected industries into hiring and capital expenditure. New US restrictions could justify cutting rates. Generalised and persistent inflation following a prolonged conflict could warrant consecutive increases. If both happened, weaker demand would itself influence how far higher costs reached consumer prices. The account contains no vote tally or assignment of probabilities to those paths. Members also recognised that demographic change, trade restructuring and adoption of AI could change potential supply over time, making the interaction more complicated than a comparison of today’s headline GDP and inflation readings (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

questions.question: Did the first-quarter GDP miss indicate weak final demand or temporary swings in government purchases and inventory?
questions.detail: Construct contributions from public spending, household consumption, housing, inventory and trade. Use the data vintage available on 10 June, then compare with later revisions. Track hours and growth across industries. A subsequent rebound concentrated in public procurement would repair the headline without demonstrating a sustained recovery in private investment or employment.

questions.question: How far did refining and logistics costs reach beyond direct petrol prices?
questions.detail: Pair the crude benchmark with refinery margins, Canadian fuel prices, freight charges and prices of exposed final products. Adjust for the previous carbon-tax change and compare with less exposed services. Determine whether businesses absorbed costs through margins or passed them on after a lag. A high crude price and elevated headline CPI alone cannot establish broad propagation.

questions.question: Did anticipated Canada–US policy divergence explain the currency move, or did global risk sentiment dominate?
questions.detail: Separate energy, US yield and Canadian data surprises during the weeks before the meeting from changes at the June decision and at publication of the summary. Compare cross rates and the trade-weighted Canadian dollar with the bilateral US dollar rate. The conclusion about imported-price pressure depends on which suppliers’ currencies moved as well as on the source of the change.
